title: The birth of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: One land, two peoples, and a British promise impossible to keep. How **1948** gave birth to the longest conflict in the Middle East.

hero.hook: How a letter written in 1917 gave birth to the longest conflict in the Middle East.

blocks.text: At the end of the 19th century, **Palestine** was a quiet province of the **Ottoman Empire**, mostly Arab and Muslim, with Christian minorities and a small, long-established Jewish community. Nothing suggested that this land would become the stage for one of the longest conflicts in the world. It all started when two national movements met and claimed the same ground: one born in Europe among Jews trying to escape persecution, the other among the Arabs of the region, who also dreamed of a country of their own. Between the two, a colonial power handed out one contradictory promise after another.

sections.title: Two nationalisms awaken in Ottoman Palestine

blocks.text: The picture changed with the rise of **[[Zionism]]** in Europe, set out by **Theodor Herzl** at a congress in Basel in 1897, in answer to growing antisemitism. For Herzl, Jews would never be safe without a state of their own.
Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, did not speak Hebrew, and he even considered Argentina as a home before settling on Palestine.

The break came during the First World War. In 1917 the British government published the **[[Balfour Declaration]]**, which promised a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine while stating that nothing should harm the rights of the communities already living there. To the Arabs of the region, that promise looked like a betrayal.

sections.title: The dead end of the British Mandate

blocks.text: After the Ottoman defeat, the League of Nations gave Britain the **Mandate for Palestine** in 1922: London was supposed both to encourage the settlement of Jews arriving from Europe and to protect the rights of the Arab population, which was the majority there.

In the 1930s, the Nazi rise to power in Germany set off a wave of Jewish immigration, the **Aliyah**: the Jewish population grew from 8% in 1918 to more than 30% before the Second World War. That alarmed the Arabs of Palestine, who rose in revolt between 1936 and 1939.
Tel Aviv, founded in 1909 on sand dunes, takes its name from a novel by Herzl: “Tel” for the ancient hill, “Aviv” for spring.

The British then capped Jewish immigration, at the very moment when the Jews of Europe were fleeing the Holocaust, which turned the Jewish militias against them. Exhausted, Britain finally handed its mandate over to the United Nations.

In November 1947, the United Nations adopted a plan to divide Palestine into two states, one Jewish and one Arab, with Jerusalem given a special international status. The Zionist leaders accepted the plan and the Arabs rejected it. A civil war broke out almost at once.

blocks.caption: On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaims the birth of the State of Israel, hours before the British Mandate ends

blocks.text: On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the birth of the **State of Israel**. The next day several Arab armies invaded to stop it, but the better organized Israeli forces pushed the offensive back and extended their control to 78% of former Mandatory Palestine.

sections.title: The Nakba and the refugee question

blocks.text: For Israelis, that victory secured their survival. For Palestinians, the event has a name: the **Nakba**, “the catastrophe.” Between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes, often hoping to return after an Arab victory.

Those refugees settled in Gaza, in the West Bank, or in neighboring countries. Israel refused to let them return, fearing the loss of its Jewish majority. In the same years, about 800,000 Jews from Arab countries moved to Israel, often under pressure.

In 1949, the United Nations created the **[[UNRWA]]** agency to help Palestinian refugees. What was meant to be temporary became permanent: no agreement fixed final borders or settled the fate of the exiles, and the absence of a Palestinian state remains at the heart of the conflict.

events.detail: Two states are proposed, and the Arabs refuse.

events.title: Independence and Nakba
events.detail: Israel is born, war breaks out, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians flee.

blocks.text: In 1947 the United Nations proposed splitting Palestine into two states. The Jews accepted, the Arabs refused. The war that followed the creation of Israel in 1948 ended in an Israeli victory and the exodus of more than 700,000 Palestinians: the start of the Nakba and of a refugee crisis that has never been resolved.
